pages.content:
All right - things are now getting serious! \
In this module on **Array Operations** - we will learn the concepts required to successfully perform beginner level array construction and manipulation required in programming problems.

- Arrays are used to store multiple items in a single variable
- Array items can be accessed by referring to their index.
  - $array[3]$ refers to the $4^{th}$ item of the array

Go to the IDE to revise the the above.

pages.title: Review problem - 1
pages.content:
Chef recorded a video explaining his favorite recipe. However, the size of the video is too large to upload on the internet. He wants to compress the video so that it has the minimum size possible. 

Chef's video has $N$ frames initially. The value of the $i^{th}$ frame is $A_i$. Chef can do the following type of operation **any** number of times:
- Choose an index $i$ $(1\le i \le N)$ such that the value of the $i^{th}$ frame is **equal** to the value of **either** of its neighbors and **remove** the $i^{th}$ frame. 

Find the **minimum** number of frames Chef can achieve.

pages.title: Introduction to the module on Strings
pages.content:
So far, we have focused on logic, integers, math. \
The module on logic building and problem solving primarily covered number operations. 

It is time to add 'Strings' to our arsenal for solving programming problems.

Lets revise some basic syntax of strings.
- Strings are a **datatype**.
  - A string is composed of characters. A single character can be any letter, any digit, symbol, etc.
  - A **binary string** is one which has only '0' and '1' as component characters
  - The character in the $i^{th}$ index of a string is represented as **S[i]**

Click in **Next** to proceed.

pages.title: Introdution to unit testing
pages.content:
We have learned about the flow of control, tracing key variables and checkpoints in the previous modules.

Using those techniques you can debug problems whose test case is given to you. \
Sometimes your submission gives an `AC` in most of the test cases but fails in a few test cases. \
Here - you need to generate your own test cases using a special technique named **Unit Testing**.

In unit testing, 
- We generate multiple `test cases` and their `expected output` in our notebook / diary / in our mind
- We then run our code on our unit test cases 
- We compare the `expected output` from our book with the `actual output` to see which test cases are failing and then try and identify the error in the code
- Fix the code and repeat the steps above till you get an `AC`

pages.title: Learning to create test cases
pages.content:
In this lesson, we will learn to create valid test cases.
For a test case to be valid it should satisfy all the test case constraints and the input format.
So you need to read those two thing carefully to create a valid test case.

Let's try to create some valid test case reading constraints and input format.

### Input
- The first line of the input contains a single integer T denoting the number of test cases. The description of 
T test cases follows.
- The first line of each test case contains three space-separated integers N, K and V.
- The second line contains N space-separated integers A1,A2,A3...AN.

### Constraints
- 1≤T≤100
- 1 ≤ N, K ≤ 100
- 1 ≤ V ≤ $10^5$
- 1 ≤ Ai ≤ $10^5$

pages.title: How to create edge test case
pages.content:
While searching for the failing test cases - you can't create a lot of test cases, since that would be time consuming.

Try and create unit tests which meet one or more of the following criteria
- Thoroughly understand the program logic, constraints and Input / Output format. 
- Identify the boundary conditions, and the upper and lower limit for input format and make test cases around it.
- Create a test case around large inputs.
- Consider the negative values in the test case.
- Consider zero input as one of the special test cases.
